query: Starting from a W–Cu composite containing W particles or interconnected W ligaments within a Cu matrix, what single intervention could overcome phase separation and interfacial void formation, thereby improving thermal conductivity relative to the untreated composite under heat-transfer and irradiation conditions relevant to joints between W-based plasma-facing materials and Cu-based cooling components? Formulate one hypothesis that states the intervention, the proposed mechanism, the predicted comparative outcome, the applicable processing and service boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: Adding 1–2 wt % Ni to the Cu phase during infiltration/hot-pressing of a W-Cu composite will form an ultrathin W–Ni interfacial layer that (i) eliminates most as-processed W/Cu micro-voids, and (ii) suppresses irradiation-induced phase separation and Kirkendall porosity, so that the through-plane thermal conductivity of the joint remains ≥90 % of its initial value after 10–100 dpa at 350–800 °C—at least 15 % higher than an otherwise identical Ni-free W-Cu composite processed and tested in the same way.
generation.material_initial_state: Porous W skeleton (≈60 vol %) infiltrated with pure Cu to make a W–Cu composite that initially contains discrete W particles/interconnected ligaments in a Cu matrix, with typical interfacial voids created during solidification.
generation.intervention: Replace the pure Cu infiltrant with a Cu–Ni alloy containing 1–2 wt % Ni and hot-press at 1050 °C for 30 min in vacuum (30 MPa).
generation.conditions: Processing: vacuum hot-press 1050 °C, 30 min, 30 MPa. Service: 350–800 °C under 5–20 MW m⁻² heat flux and neutron/ion irradiation producing 10–100 dpa.
generation.structural_mediator: ≈5 nm continuous W–Ni intermetallic (WNi_x) layer that improves chemical bonding and acts as a defect sink at the W/Cu interface.
generation.mechanism: Ni lowers the W/Cu interfacial energy, producing liquid-phase assisted diffusion bonding that heals processing pores. The resulting W–Ni layer traps irradiation-generated vacancies and interstitials, reducing void swelling and preventing W/Cu phase separation, thereby preserving continuous Cu heat-conduction paths.
generation.predicted_outcome: Room-temperature thermal conductivity: baseline 220 ± 10 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (Ni-free) vs ≥250 ± 10 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ (with Ni). After 10–100 dpa at 600 °C the Ni-modified composite retains ≥90 % of its initial conductivity, while the baseline falls to ≤70 %. Interfacial void density is at least 50 % lower in the Ni-modified material both pre- and post-irradiation.
generation.baseline: W–Cu composite fabricated identically but with pure Cu infiltrant (0 wt % Ni).
generation.boundary: Effective for 0.5–3 wt % Ni, processing 1000–1100 °C, W fraction 50–70 vol %. Above 800 °C service temperature or >3 wt % Ni, excessive Ni diffusion into Cu may re-introduce Kirkendall porosity and negate benefits.
generation.uncertainty: Direct high-flux irradiation data for W–Ni–Cu interfaces are scarce; magnitude of long-term conductivity retention may vary by ±20 %.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of discs (10 mm × 2 mm): (a) W–Cu (0 wt % Ni) and (b) W–Cu–1 wt % Ni processed as specified. Measure thermal conductivity (laser-flash) at RT and 600 °C before irradiation. Irradiate both sets with 5 MeV Cu⁺ ions to 10 dpa at 600 °C. Re-measure conductivity and quantify interfacial void fraction via FIB-SEM tomography and TEM.
measurements: Thermal diffusivity and specific heat (laser-flash) to derive k
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Ni-modified specimens (i) show <10 % increase in initial thermal conductivity relative to baseline or (ii) retain ≤80 % of their initial conductivity after irradiation, OR (iii) do not exhibit ≥50 % lower interfacial void fraction, the hypothesis is falsified.
